OA.2 Argentina

Section 5 of the paper calibrates the model with informal households to Argentina before the coverage reforms and reads the reforms as a rise of the universal pension \(\epsilon\); appendix D gives the survey, the identifying formulas and the sources. This chapter holds the calibration under both treatments of the taste for leisure, the reform at every intertemporal elasticity of the model’s grid, the equilibrium over pension designs, and the calibration at every IES.

OA.2.1 Calibration

The paper takes the taste for leisure common to the four formal quartiles and pins its level by the average formal workweek, so relative hours are a prediction. The alternative identifies one \(X_i\) per quartile from the survey’s relative hours. Only the productivity and leisure parameters differ between the two: the aggregate targets, and every result of section 5, are the same under both.

OA.2.2 The reform

The first table is the paper’s: the effect in 2010 of raising \(\epsilon\) to the universal level, with the tax rate held at its pre-reform path and chosen politically. The second prints the paths of the tax rate, the savings rate and the workweek before and after the reform.

\(\cdot\)

Calibration

Table 2 of the paper: the effect in 2010 of raising the universal pension \(\epsilon\) to the level at which informal retirees receive the benefit of the least productive formal workers, unanticipated and permanent. The first row is the pre-reform economy; the second holds the tax rate at its pre-reform path and so isolates the response of households; the third lets the electorate reset the tax. Taxes rise, because the reform moves benefits toward informal retirees, who are poorer than formal ones and value them more at the margin, and savings and hours fall a little; with the tax held fixed, formal savings rise instead, since informal households now hold a claim on the system and save less.

Under the vector-\(X_i\) calibration this exhibit is identical to the common-\(X\) one to the last printed digit, as the comparison in section OA.3.2 records: the calibration is block recursive, so the aggregates the reform moves do not depend on how the taste for leisure is split across the quartiles.

The same reform along the path: the tax rate, the savings rate and the workweek in every model period from the reform year on, on the pre-reform path and on the reform path side by side. The tax response builds over the first periods, because informal households, now covered, save less for retirement and as retirees demand more taxation; section 5 of the paper quotes the response one period on.

Under the vector-\(X_i\) calibration this exhibit is identical to the common-\(X\) one to the last printed digit, as the comparison in section OA.3.2 records: the calibration is block recursive, so the aggregates the reform moves do not depend on how the taste for leisure is split across the quartiles.

OA.2.3 The reform across the intertemporal elasticity

Section 5 reads the reform across the intertemporal elasticity of substitution (IES) \(\rho\) from the figure, which is the paper’s; the model is solved on a grid of sixteen values. The table prints the reform at every point of the grid. Click a point of the figure for its row.

\(\cdot\)

Calibration

Figure 5.2 of the paper: the effect of the reform on the tax rate, the savings rate, the workweek and the ratio of informal to formal savings, on impact and one period on, at every IES of the grid, each economy recalibrated to the same pre-reform targets. Below an IES of one the responses are dampened, and at the lowest elasticities the tax response on impact reverses, since the young resist taxation more and the calibration needs a heavier political weight of the old to reproduce the observed tax rate; between one and two the responses stay close to the log benchmark.

Under the vector-\(X_i\) calibration this exhibit is identical to the common-\(X\) one to the last printed digit, as the comparison in section OA.3.2 records: the calibration is block recursive, so the aggregates the reform moves do not depend on how the taste for leisure is split across the quartiles.

The values behind the figure’s short-run series, one row per point of the grid: the post-reform tax rate, the change in the savings rate and the workweek in the reform year. The pre-reform row is common to every IES, because each is recalibrated to the same targets; the pre-reform savings rate is not a target and varies with the IES, so its column is a change.

Under the vector-\(X_i\) calibration this exhibit is identical to the common-\(X\) one to the last printed digit, as the comparison in section OA.3.2 records: the calibration is block recursive, so the aggregates the reform moves do not depend on how the taste for leisure is split across the quartiles.

OA.2.4 The equilibrium over pension designs

The equilibrium in 2010 over a grid of designs \((\epsilon, \theta)\), each point an economy that has always had that design, with the pre-reform calibration and the universal system at the calibrated \(\theta\) marked. The tax rate rises with \(\epsilon\) and falls with \(\theta\), the savings rate and the workweek fall with \(\epsilon\) and rise with \(\theta\), and the savings of informal relative to formal households fall with \(\epsilon\). Between the two markers the tax rate rises by more than it does on impact in section 5 of the paper, because the savings of informal households have adjusted to the universal system; the difference is close to the reform’s effect by 2040 (OA.2.2). The grid itself can be downloaded from the figure’s source.

\(\cdot\)

Calibration

OA.2.5 The calibration across the intertemporal elasticity

The table and the figure print the parameters solved jointly with the equilibrium path at every IES of the grid, which show how the calibration absorbs a change in \(\rho\): matching the targets at an IES of 0.6 or below takes a thirty-year discount factor above one.

\(\cdot\)

Calibration

Four panels are parameters solved at each IES and two are predictions of the calibration, the savings rate and the informal savings ratio in 2010. The discount factor and the political weight of the old both fall as the IES rises, the second because the young resist taxation less and a lighter weight of the old reproduces the observed tax rate; the savings rate falls, the informal savings ratio rises, and the informal productivity and taste for leisure barely move.

Under the vector-\(X_i\) calibration the discount factor, the political weight of the old, the savings rate and the informal savings ratio are those of the common \(X\) at every IES; only the informal productivity and taste for leisure take other values, and they too barely move with the IES.
